Because the curvature object that AdaFish actually needs turns out to be cheap to handle in the low-rank PEFT setting. AdaFish's key observation is that the generalized Fisher information matrix associated with low-rank decomposition-based fine-tuning is **either low-rank or extremely small-scaled**, and this matrix is shown to be equivalent to the Hessian [1]. So the quantity playing the role of the Hessian never has the full quadratic dimension that normally makes second-order methods prohibitive — it can be stored and manipulated at low cost, which is what lets AdaFish use second-order (curvature) updates to speed up training while remaining competitive with AdamW [1].

Contrast this with the general case: estimating Hessian information is typically expensive in function evaluations, which is exactly why methods like ZO-SAH go to lengths such as restricting estimation to random two-dimensional subspaces [10]. AdaFish avoids that problem structurally rather than by approximation, since the low-rank structure is intrinsic to the fine-tuning parameterization itself [1].
